newsitem.title: BELGIUM: YEARENDER - BELGIAN RATES TO RISE, SPREADS STEADY.
newsitem.headline: YEARENDER - BELGIAN RATES TO RISE, SPREADS STEADY.

text.p: Belgian bond and money market yields are set to rise gradually on the back of an economic recovery in 1997, but benchmark yield spreads over German Bunds should remain at around current levels, economists said.

Belgian 10-year benchmark bond yields are seen rising to 6.25 to 6.75 percent by the end of 1997 from the current 5.95 percent, while three-month money market yields will go up to 3.20 to 3.50 percent from the current 3.02 percent.
With no elections upcoming next year and a 1997 budget judged credible enough for single currency membership, yield premiums over Germany are expected to remain at current levels.
"I see no significant change in yield spreads over Germany," BBL economist Peter Vanden Houte said.
Ten-year Belgian yields are currently at a historicaly low nine basis points over Germany. Short-term Belgian yields are at par with or just below German yields.

Generale Bank chief economist Peter Praet also saw spreads remaining at current levels, but warned that there could be increased volatility in the spring, when the government is due to review the 1997 budget and the social security system.
"We know that there is a significant deterioration in health care spending, which will have to be adressed," Praet said. The budget is traditionally reviewed in February-March.

A second important deadline is April when the government's power to reform the social security system by decree, granted in July, expires. Decree powers for measures for the 1997 budget end in August.

But while rule by decree makes passing measures through parliament easier, it cannot prevent social unrest. Praet and Vanden Houte said strikes and street protest could block the long-awaited reform of the civil servants' pension system.
"The one thing I fear is the civil workers' pension reform. Any upheaval over that could lead to a temporary widening of yields spreads over Germany," Vanden Houte said.
But he added the reform was not absolutely necessary to comply with single currency membership criteria, and that any reform would probably be gradual.
Economists agreed that, due to the absence of major domestic factors, Belgian rates would mainly track German and U.S. rates.

"World bond yields are set to rise, due to higher growth in the U.S. and Europe, but the rise should be limited," Praet said. Long-term yields had reached their lowest point in the cycle. He did not expect the Bundesbank to increase rates until late in 1997.

"The yield curve will become even steeper than it already is as there is no reason for short-term rates to rise while bond yields will tend to rise on the back of a stronger German and U.S. economy," Gemeentekrediet chief economist Eddy Pletinck said.

Vanden Houte added the very steepness of the European yield curve would cushion any sell-off in the bond markets as a switch into cash is less attactive for European investors than for American investors.
The U.S. yield curve is much flatter, with three-month yields at 4.99 percent and 10-year yields at 6.33 percent.
